lines.text: אטט 39 אי
sinew, string. Once Prov. 7, 16 tapes-
try, coverings, of Egyptian yarn, which
was distinguished for its firmness and
beauty. Comp. Celsii Hierob. I. 89 sq.
A. Schultens compares Gr. ὀθόνη, ὀθό-
νιον, linen cloth.
* אָטַט a root not in use. 1. i. q. أَطَّ
to utter a gentle sound, to murmur,
spoken of the sighing of the camel when
weary; also of the rumbling of the
bowels when one is hungry, τρύζειν.
See Comment. on Is. 19, 3.
2. to go softly, gently, see אַט no. 2.
* אָטַם to shut, to close, to stop, e. g.
the mouth, the ears, Prov. 17, 28. 21, 13.
windows closed, sc. with bars or lattices,
which being let into the walls or beams
could not be opened and shut at pleas-
ure. Sept. θυρίδες δικτυωταί, Symm.
τοξικαί. Comp. 1 K. 6, 4. Kindr. is Arab.
أَطَمَ to cover a window with a curtain.
Hiph. id. Ps. 58, 5.
* אָטַן obsol. root, perh. to bind, to bind
together, kindr. with אָטַם. Arab. أَطُنٌ
tent-cords.—Hence אֵטוּן.
* אָטַר fut. יֶאְטַר, to shut, to close,
once Ps. 69, 16. Arab. أطر to shut
in, to enclose. Kindred roots are אָצַר,
חָצַר, עָצַר.—Hence the two following:
אָטֵר (shut up, bound, perh. dumb)
Ater, pr. n. m. a) Ezra 2, 16. Neh. 7,
אִטֵּר m. adj. (r. אָטַר) shut up, bound,
i. e. impeded. Judg. 3, 15. 20, 16 אִטֵּר
יַד יְמִינוֹ impeded as to his right hand,
i. e. who cannot use the right hand free-
ly, and hence i. q. left-handed. Arab.
أَطَرَ Conj. V, to be impeded; comp.
عقل to bind, to tie, transferred also to
the tongue, like Engl. tongue-tied.
* אַי, constr. אֵי 1. Interrog. adverb,
where? c. suff. אַיֶּכָּה where art thou?
Gen. 3, 9. אַיּוֹ where is he? Ex. 2, 20.
אַיָּם where are they? Is. 19, 12. More
freq. with He parag. אַיֵּה q. v.—This
particle seems to have arisen by drop-
ping the Nun from אַיִן II, (q. v. in מֵאַיִן
whence?) and this again seems to have
been originally the same as the nega-
tive אַיִן I; just as many other negative
words have also passed over to an in-
terrogative power; comp. Lat. ne, Germ.
nicht wahr? Engl. not so? Hence אַיִן
pr. he is not there, not present, i. q. אֵינֶנּוּ,
comp. Job 14, 10; and interrog. is he not
there? q. d. where is he? In this way
אַיֵּה no. I and II become closely related.
Comp. Heb. Gram. § 150. no. 1 ult. In
Arabic أَيٌّ has passed over into an in-
terrog. pron. who? f. أَيَّةٌ; and the same
also is Eth. አይ. Comp. Germ. wo?
Engl. who?
2. As a mere sign of interrogation, put
before adverbs and pronouns in order to
give them an interrogative power; just
as אֲשֶׁר gives them a relative sense.
Comp. Germ. wovon? for von welchem?
Engl. wherefore? i. q. for what? Hence
a) אֵי זֶה, which? what? but always with
reference to place (except in Ecc. 11,
6), 1 K. 13, 12 אֵי זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ הָלַךְ what way
went he? (Or perh. i. q. Lat. ubi viæ?
quorsum viæ? see under אֵי מִזֶּה in lett.
Also without interrogation, Jer. 6, 16.
Ecc. 11, 6. Elsewhere i. q. where?
(from זֶה here,) Job 28, 12. Esth. 7, 5.
Sometimes written in one word, אֵיזֶה,
q. v. b) אֵי מִזֶּה from what? whence?
(from מִזֶּה thence,) Gen. 16, 8. 1 Sam.
30, 13. Jon. 1, 8 אֵי מִזֶּה עָם אַתָּה from
what people art thou? 2 Sam. 15, 2 אֵי
מִזֶּה עִיר אַתָּה from what city art thou?
strictly Lat. ‘undenam populi? undenam
urbis?’ as Plaut. unde gentium? Odyss.
1. 170 πόθεν ἀνδρῶν. c) אֵי לָזֹאת where-
fore? why? from לָזֹאת therefore, Jer. 5, 7.
Note. With certain other particles
אֵי is joined more closely, so as to coa-
lesce with them into one word, as אֵיךְ,
אֵיכָה, אֵיכֹה, אֵיפֹה, q. v. The same use
of this particle is found in Syr. ܐܰܝܟܰܢܳܐ
in what way? how? ܐܰܝܡܶܟܳܐ whence?
ܐܰܝܢܳܐ who? Chald. אֵידַיִן who then? אֵידָם
id. Eth. አይቴ where? how?—In Prov.
31, 4 Keri וּלְרוֹזְנִים אֵי שֵׁכָר, render: nor
for princes [to say], Where is strong
drink? See in אַי no. 1.
I. אִי contr. for אֱוִי, (as כִּי for כְּוִי, דִּי
for דְּוַי, comp. Lehrg. p. 510,) m. perhaps

line_status.note: The leftmost letter of the left header word is printed with the open top and inward curl of a tet, identical to the middle letter, not the closed square of a final mem; the header reads אטט (apparent typesetting error for אטם) — Reading B matches what is printed.

The first word is printed defectively: after the dageshed lamed there is a holem dot directly above it, and the only vav in the word is the one before the final tav — five letters (ח ל נ ו ת), not six. Reading A's extra vav (חַלּוֹנוֹת) is not on the page.
The mark over the ṭāʾ is a plain fatḥa stroke, with no shadda printed; Reading B's doubled ṭāʾ (أَطَّمَ) is not in the image. Form I أَطَمَ as in Reading A.
Final nūn carries the printed double-ḍamma tanwīn (ٌ), not a sukūn as in B; the hamza over the alif has a fatḥa stroke, not a ḍamma. A matches the print.
The Arabic is printed with hamza on the alif (أطر) but no fatḥa vowel marks over ṭā or rā; Reading A's fully vocalised أَطَرَ adds vowels not on the page.

Under the aleph the print shows a qamets (short vertical stroke with a bar), not a single hireq dot; the tet carries a two-dot tsere and no visible dagesh. Reading A matches the printed form (even though the expected lemma is אִטֵּר, Judg. 3:15).
The final letter is he (ה, open top-left corner, flat top bar), not final nun (ן); two dots under the yod (tsere) rather than hiriq. Context (“where is he?”) confirms אַיֵּה “where?”.
The mark above the shadda over ي has a hooked tail (two-stroke damma form), i.e. dammatan ٌ, not a plain damma ُ — so Reading A (أَيٌّ, ayyun) matches the print.
The final ta marbuta carries tanwin damm (ٌ, the damma with a tail), not a plain damma; the print also spaces "who ?" and " ;" as in A.
After the Ethiopic አይ only a single dot is printed (a full stop), not the two-dot Ethiopic word separator ፡ of Reading B; the question mark after "wo" is spaced as in Reading A.
Printed has qamets under ע of עָם (B right, A wrong) but patach under א of אַתָּה (A right, B wrong); neither reading matches both points.
The vowel under the aleph of אַתָּה is a short horizontal patach (same form as in line 1's אַתָּה), not a qamets with a descending stem; Reading B's אָתָּה is wrong.

The Syriac word is printed in Serto with Western Greek-style vowel glyphs (ptāḥā ܰ on olaph, rbāṣā ܶ on mim, the small "o"-shaped zqāphā ܳ on kaph/final olaph), not the Eastern dot-vowels of Reading B. Letters ܐܝܡܟܐ agree in both readings.

The Syriac is printed in Serto with Western vowel signs (wedge-shaped pthaha over the first alef, ring-shaped zqapha over nun), matching Reading A, not B's Eastern points. But the Chaldee word is clearly printed plene with five letters, אֵידַיִן (a yod with hiriq visible between dalet and nun), matching Reading B, not A's אֵידֵין.

Final word: the letter is dalet (top bar projects right past the stem, matching the דְּוִי on the next line), so A's resh is wrong; but the vowel beneath is a single dot (hiriq), not a patah, so B's דַּי is also wrong. Printed is דִּי (dagesh dot visible in the dalet), parallel to the following "for דְּוִי".

The first Hebrew letter carries a dagesh (dot inside) and sheva, so it is דּ not ר, and the vav has a patach (horizontal stroke) beneath it, not a hiriq — matching Reading B and completing "דַּי for דְּוַי" begun at the end of line 3.
